text: The 6900XT makes no sense for gamers but for people editing 4k, 6k, 8k and 16k video, it makes sense. While the framerates in games are terrible by comparison,  the 6900XT actually beats both the 6800XT and the 3090 by large margins in everything but certain encoding applications. When editing 4k, your card needs a minimum of 10Gb to even start to be efficient.  6k needs 12 Gb and 8k needs 16Gb. At 16k, the 3090 takes over as it is the only card that has enough RAM to be efficient. We do a lot of 4k and 8k and time is money. The 6900XTs we have do a great job compared to the 6800XT machines on 8k and we have one machine dedicated to 16k that has a 3090. We don't see as much 16k yet as we expected,  largely because storage requirements are outrageous but it is coming. How broadcasters are going to adopt it is an open question as bandwidth is limited and decompression and compression algorithms aren't good enough (fast enough) to send the signals over current networks. The current  digital broadcast system, cable channels, etc. was not set up with the kind of future proofing that was needed. Our networks internally had to go all fiber and they still have trouble keeping up. But as larger screens become common, in order to maintain pixel density,  you have to go to higher resolutions. A 4k resolution is necessary on a 32 inch monitor just to maintain the same pixel density as 1440 on a 27 inch monitor.  For very large screens or projections, 8k is necessary just to have the same pixel density as a 1440 27 inch monitor.  For really huge presentations, 16k is now necessary to get an impressive image. We now have commercial projectors that run  on all fiber networks at 24k. Editing the presentation video is going to be a real challenge, not only for networks but for storage. The amounts of data are vast and have to be moved in real time. We're having trouble at 8k.

text:
Even though the price-to-performance is pretty awful, it's very impressive that the 6900 XT consistently runs 10% faster than 10% fewer CUs on the same architecture at similar clocks (outside of CPU bottlenecks), especially when you compare that to Nvidia getting a smaller performance gain from a 20% increase in shaders between the 3080 and 3090, and the absolutely awful scaling of GCN above 40 CUs. This bodes very well for AIB models with coolers that could let the card run at close to 2.8GHz, and for RDNA3, if AMD can maintain this scaling with a chiplet-based design.

The RX 6900 XT ROG Strix LC has a decent chance of being the fastest graphics card of the generation, with the exception of ray tracing and DLSS, and even then AMD's "Super Resolution" might negate most of the advantages of DLSS once it finally comes out.

text:
It seems like modern games can make better use of AMD gpu's. 
That said, the industry in general (looking at both games and professional software devs) needs to go back supporting Open standards (aka, OpenCL etc. - no licensing fees, and you can get everything done like on NV hw just without proprietary features - open source works on NV too, and arguably better than proprietary stuff).

I agree RT performance on AMD gpu's is not as good, but to be fair, I'm not hung up on Raytracing because most of the time, you don't even notice it to begin with... so I don't really miss it.
Plus, AMD's RT is done via open standards, so drivers can improve on this, and if games implement better optimizations for AMD gpu's... its likely RT performance on AMD gpu's will improve (by how much, not sure).

And AMD has 'super resolution' (their version of DLSS) coming soon (aka early next year if I'm not mistaken), so things should get interesting with that too.
Again, not bothered because RDNA 2 seems to have the raw power in it which software needs to be coded properly to make use of it in the first place... and for the price, you get better efficiency and 'price/performance' ratio on AMD than on NV.

text:
@Hardwareunboxed  So why is this point beaten to death every video? Nearly everyone has a hobby or interest where an outsider can look in and think you're absolutely flushing your money down the toilet. You literally called the people who'd buy the halo product dumb, even though you do show that there still is a performance increase. That last 10% or so in increased performance is exponentially more expensive to produce than the lower 90%. There is more of a performance difference in the 6800xt to 6900xt or the 3080 to 3090 for the difference in % cost than there is in performance difference from the ~$20k YZF-R1M and the $1mil+ MotoGP YZF-M1.

I don't get where the bashing of halo products comes from. I perfectly do understand that for cost/performance, it's not the most efficient. But if absolute best raw performance is your goal, then these halo cards are your best bet. While it can be argued that the tier below can be OCed to reach similar performance, it can once against be stated that you can just OC these halo cards. Although I suspect that the odd OCing performance with the 6900xt reviewers are seeing are a bit more of a driver issue than hardware issue. If everyone was looking for a pure cost/performance outlook, most people pinching pennies wouldn't even be looking at the upper end of the 30 series or the current 6000 series at all. I feel that as you start transitioning into the enthusiast grade hardware, cost to performance starts going down the hierarchy in reference to performance.

text:
I can sort of see a couple of somewhat niche use cases for this card.

1: Somebody who wants to minmax a $1200-1300 build. If you can find one of these at msrp or a bit below it, that's about the maximum amount of GPU you can get at that budget, once you throw a budget cpu, motherboard, ram and all that in there. Not a terribly common scenario, but I can see that appealing to somebody.

2: Somebody who wants or needs to upgrade right now and has the money, but who wants to hold out until ray tracing doesn't require you to slice your resolution or framerate in half.

3: Somebody building on some kind of budget 4-5 years down the line. 1080ti is still an absolute monster today, and when they're available for around £400-450 they represent a solid option if you're making a build today. Thusly, I should imagine that a few years down the line, a used 6900xt might make a good GPU for people looking to build on some kind of a budget.

text: Still waiting on any benchmark site to test RT with upscaling + RIS on AMD.  DLSS is nothing more than an upscaling solution.  Any upscaling solution can be used.  None of them are perfect visually.
author: @JasonDominus

text: Eh, not really. With AI upscaling some detail can be recreated, with just upscaling existing data is just rescaled, it's not even a competition for DLSS 2.0.
author: @MLWJ1993

text:
@MLWJ1993  it's demonstratively available that they are in the close in IQ with different strengths and weaknesses.  All minor on both vendors.  Also the   performance uplift comes from the resolution upscale.  The AI upscaling is only IQ.  Performance is equal.  

My main point is people think DLSS is a unique feature when it's just in the umbrella of upscaling solutions.  Ie upscaling + some way to regain IQ.
author: @JasonDominus

text:
@JasonDominus  you don't "regain" any IQ by sharpening a lower resolution & then blowing it up to a higher size, that's not how IQ works. It's all just resized data that was already there. You gain exactly nothing in image quality & it straight up sucks in movement.

With something filling in gaps with new data (accurate or not) you gain something plus DLSS 2.0 handles moving elements a lot better compared to a sharpen & upscale since generally sharpened data introduces lots of shimmering which I genuinely find annoying. I rather have things slightly more blurred compared to sharpened to the limit in order to not lose more data during upscaling.
author: @MLWJ1993

text:
@MLWJ1993  regain is purely a semantic choice of words.  Scaling has to fill in the blanks because it isn't native.  My original point was that these solutions are under the same umbrella.  Just different techniques.  I'm glad we agree.  

 It's funny you devolved your argument into a preference argument in the end.  Then again it's all you have.
author: @JasonDominus

text:
@JasonDominus  Look you do you & believe there's "new" data in your prehistoric upscales using just "math" based on original data.

You clearly don't even begin to fathom how inferior that approach is for scaling to higher resolutions. It will never get any decent results & at worst destroy the image by sharpening pixels beforehand.

At best AI upscaling nets a perfect representation of what it's supposed to be, at worst it gets it wrong & makes things represent something (slightly) different from intended. Both however are results that show new data, not interpolations of samples taken from the low resolution source.

Also with training AI upscaling gets better & more accurate over time, meanwhile a mathematical approach is never going to get better unless you change the math which is never going to be versatile enough to account for all different objects in a scene...

text:
Devices like the 3090 and the 6900XT have never made sense value wise. Nor were they ever supposed to. They are first and formost halo products. The premium gap between ie. the 3080 and 3090, is traditionally 80-90% bragging tax, 10-20% performance return on investment.

Still. If you're actually looking for some kind of performance/value among these halo products before us, versus their "normal line-up top dog" (3080, 3800XT) - 6900XT seems to be the clear choice. With it's ~55% MSRP premium over the 6800XT, versus the 3090's 115%(!!) premium over the 3080. In the Rsdeon equation, you're basically stacking another half a 6800XT on top, to reach the 6900XT. In case of team green however, we're literally talking a whole entire extra 3080 on top of your first 3080, and almost a 3300X, or a good-deal 1TB QLC SSD, to step up from the 3080 to the 3090.

IMO, none of these two halo products actually make sense. But if you're the kind that buy these types of halo products, especially the 3090, then by the time that small performance improvement you get for the upgrade from the 3080, start making a real difference - you'll likely have longe since moved on to something else.

text:
​ @PeterNjeim  Hey Peter, I didn't call you dumb at all. I was actually talking about the general smartphone audience, but I guess the proper word to use is uninformed or ignorant. I am an adult, not some 13 year old kid trying to throw insults on the internet. 

Now all that being said, and with all due respect, what you are saying isn't quite right. Names have a meaning behind them, and often also a value associated with them. For example, Apple is known for making premium devices, and while they might offer cheaper new iPhones, they WILL never make sub $200 devices. Same thing with Ferrari, the cheapest Ferrari you can get it is $260k. 

You see, if Apple started making cheap phones or Ferrari starting making family cars at $30k their image would take a hit, so when someone says I got the latest iPhone, or on the other extreme, I bought a new Ferrari, you know there is money/value and performance behind those titles/brands.

Going back to Nvidia. Since Nvidia started using the modern model numbers (xx10 - xx90), it was always understood that each number was a placement in the stack. In some older Nvidia generations (https://www.wikiwand.com/en/List_of_Nvidia_graphics_processing_units) they had cards at each tier of the stack, so it was common sense to associate the number with a tier, performance and price. If 1 is the lowest number, and 9 is the highest, 4-5 is in the middle, hence 1-3 are low tiers, 4-6 are mid tiers, and 7-9 are high tiers. 

Later down the line they introduced "Ti" as a mid point between tiers (6.5, or 7.5 if you will), but often the performance difference of Tis in the mid tiers and the beginning of high tiers wasn't that significant (60ti, 70ti). On the other hand, the 80ti was the highest model of the line/generation, and often came with a bump in price and performance. Last generation they introduced the "Super" tier, which realistically is another word for Ti.

So far I believe I am making sense. So, fast forward to 2018, with the introduction of the RTX series, Nvidia decided to skip all the low tiers, and the beginning of the mid tier (tiers 1-5). I am assuming they did this as a way to make more money by not giving people the option to buy ACTUAL low tier cards, and also since all of their cards had the new "ray tracing capability" they couldn't simply just slap the RTX name on a 2050 or below because the RTX performance would have been even shittier than the rest of the 2000 series which was already bad in that aspect. This is why when the RTX 2000 series came out they released an 1660ti soon after, which was basically a rtx 2050 without the RTX component relatively speaking.

Now as you can see I am not confused about the names at all. If Nvidia decides to release an rtx 3030, 3040, 3050 and 3060 with completive performance and price that would be great,  but given the current trend of the last two generations and their competitor (AMD), I don't see that happening. And I get the feeling that they are trying to get people to accept that mid tier cards (50, 50ti, 60, 60ti) are the new low tier (as you said earlier), while also bumping the price to what before was consider the beginning of high tier (xx70). So I am not getting things confused at all as I am quite familiar with the market, it is Nvidia and by extension AMD who are trying to get consumers to pay more with each generation.

For over a decade the highest tier Nvidia had to offer outside of SLI GPUs never went past $700 msrp, and in one generation it went up to $1200 msrp. And this trickled down to the xx7, and x6 cards, and all their TI and Super variants.  While the 3080 is at somewhat reasonable price when compared to previous generations, the % jump in price for the xx60, and xx70 tiers when compared to before 2018 is out of whack. A simple msrp google search for the last 8 or so generations will show that. 

Also, while there is probably not price fixing in a "shady corporate meeting" type of way, if a competitor bumps the prices and makes a profit I (as a company) will be forced to do the same, and vice-versa. Which is why the AMD GPUs cost the same as Nvidia; why sell GPUs at a good price to perf ratio when the competition is able to bump the prices and make a huge profit, I might as well cash in too, right? <--- most company's logic 

I hope that my whole essay made sense, feel free to disagree with me.

text:
Dilet  "RX 580 was the "Big Polaris," and the 5500XT was "small Navi." Maybe the architectural improvements weren't enough to outweigh the smaller GPU."
There was no "Big Polaris", Polaris was only low-end and midrange. Vega 56/64 was AMD's attempt at making a high-end version of Polaris. In terms of transistor count, the RX 580 is smaller than the RX 5500 XT, so there aren't any "architectural improvements" to be outweighed, the architecture got worse.

Navi scales exceptionally well at high CU counts, and in that sense it's better than Polaris/Vega/GCN, but it's terrible at the low-end in terms of performance per transistor, which is why I'm not at all surprised that AMD are still sticking with Vega for their mobile and desktop APUs.

I think AMD should have die-shrunk Polaris to 7nm instead of making Navi 14, but it's possible that they expected better scaling during development, or that the narrower memory and PCIe buses and better efficiency were a more significant cost saving than the silicon they would have saved from using a smaller die.

text:
@Talishar  "The margins on these GPUs, even for Nvidia and AMD, are very small"
Their profit figures say otherwise. Moore's law is slowing down, but it's not completely dead yet, and there are multiple potential post-silicon transistor designs (e.g. NVCTs, and designs based on carbon nanotubes) which could reboot it again. Development gets more expensive, but economy of scale continues to ramp up as demand for silicon increases from 5G, AI, and IOT devices.

text:
Pixel Shader batches are statically split in the central command dispatcher per-shader engine, so into 4 equally sized batches. Those are then split in half in each shader engine and assigned to the two shader arrays, so all shader arrays get the same sized work unit. Issue is half the shader arrays on the 6900 XT have 5 WGPs, while half have 4 WGPs, but due to the batches being the same, that extra WGP is never used for pixel shading. The OS specifically disable that extra WGP to give the card extra power to clock higher.

For pixel shading, the 6800 XT is a 64 CU card. For compute (which is ALSO in use in games!) it is a 72 CU card. So that is why  the 6900XT is a bit more of ajump than expected.

text:
@DeadNoob451  Guys please.
RT is not a Nvidia thing. It is not a proprietary technology.
RT is a rendering method, just like rasterization and it has been in use for decades on movies and renders.
Real time RT is the next step, no matter which vendor "made" it first. And the reason is really simple, it is "plug and play". In Rasterization a lot of work much be done to "fake" effects.
Do you want GI? it is baked. Do you want "real time" GI? You need light probes.
Do you want reflections? SSR. Do you want more accurate reflections? You need a camera looking at the opposite side of the object and transform that image into a texture.
Do you want all that in RT? Just enable RT.

Don't let others fool you. There was a time where games didn't have shadows, didn't have shaders and all of that came to an immense cost in performance when first implemented.
